result.derivedSpec: count_labels(s) returns exactly (number of raw 0x2E '.' bytes in s) + 1, with no special cases at all: the empty string yields 1, "." yields 2, ".." yields 3, and leading, trailing, and consecutive empty labels are each counted individually (".a." -> 3, "a..b" -> 3). Matching is purely byte-wise on 0x2E, so multi-byte dot look-alikes (U+3002, U+FF0E) and the overlong encoding \xc0\xae contribute nothing while a bare 0x2E inside invalid UTF-8 does count; there is no length clamping or cap, and the int counter cannot overflow because a single argv entry is limited to 131071 bytes.

`to_ascii(s)` returns the literal 4 bytes "xn--" concatenated with a byte-wise C-locale lowercased copy of s (only bytes 0x41..0x5A shift by +0x20; every other byte, including UTF-8 lead/continuation bytes and invalid UTF-8, passes through untouched). The prefix is added unconditionally with no ACE-prefix detection, no punycode transformation, no dot/label awareness, and no length limit, so to_ascii("") == "xn--" and to_ascii("XN--A") == "xn--xn--a"; it is locale-insensitive because the driver never calls setlocale.

idna::normalize(s) is a pure forwarding thunk to idna::to_lower(s) (disassembly at 0x403490 tail-calls 0x403404 with the sret pointer and argument unchanged), and to_lower is std::transform(begin,end,begin,::tolower) with each char sign-extended to int and only the low result byte stored back; since the binary never calls setlocale, the "C" locale applies and exactly the bytes 0x41-0x5A ('A'-'Z') are shifted by +32 while every other byte — including UTF-8 continuation bytes, invalid UTF-8, whitespace, and dots — passes through verbatim, with no Unicode/NFC/NFD normalization, no whitespace trimming, no trailing-dot stripping, and no length truncation. Therefore field 10 is byte-for-byte identical to field 9 for every possible input and can never differ from it.

`is_ascii_domain(s)` walks the whole std::string byte-by-byte and returns false on the first byte that is negative as a signed char (any byte >= 0x80), else true; it applies no length cap, no dot/label rules and no "xn--" special-casing, so the empty string is vacuously true (field 7 = 1), 0x00-0x7f are accepted and 0x80-0xff rejected regardless of position. Confirmed at 0x403183 where the loop body is `movzbl (%rax),%eax; mov %al,-0x9(%rbp); cmpb $0x0,-0x9(%rbp); jns continue` with `mov $0x0,%eax` on fallthrough and `mov $0x1,%eax` at loop exit - a signed sign test against 0, not a literal 0x80 compare; field 8 (is_idn_domain) is its exact negation (`xor $0x1,%eax`).

is_valid_label(s) returns true iff the string is non-empty and its BYTE length is at most 63 — i.e. `!s.empty() && s.length() <= 63` applied to the WHOLE input string, never to dot-separated labels, with no character-class rules at all (dots, hyphens, underscores, spaces, control bytes, and invalid UTF-8 are all accepted as ordinary bytes). Confirmed in the disassembly at 0x403144: `call empty; xor $0x1; je fail; call length; cmp $0x3f,%rax; ja fail; mov $1`.

`is_idn_domain(s)` returns exactly `!is_ascii_domain(s)`, where `is_ascii_domain(s)` is true iff every byte of `s` has its high bit clear (`(signed char)c >= 0`, i.e. byte < 0x80), with the empty string vacuously ASCII; so field 8 is 1 iff `s` contains at least one byte in 0x80..0xFF and 0 otherwise, with no dependence on length, dot placement, `xn--` prefixes, or UTF-8 validity. The disassembly confirms it literally as `call is_ascii_domain; xor $0x1,%eax`, and since `is_ascii_domain` only ever returns literal 0 or 1, field 8 is a provably exact negation of field 7 for every possible input.

`punycode_decode(s)` does no punycode arithmetic: it returns `s.substr(4)` if and only if `s.find("xn--") == 0` (case-sensitive, prefix-anchored, byte-level, with no minimum-length guard so the 4-byte input "xn--" yields the empty string), and otherwise returns `s` byte-for-byte unchanged — including invalid UTF-8, dots, and arbitrarily long input. Its machine code at 0x40309c is instruction-identical to `to_unicode` at 0x40300a (same "xn--" literal at 0x406069, same `find(...)==0` test, same `substr(4, npos)`), so the two functions are indistinguishable on every possible input.

is_valid_domain(s) returns true if and only if the raw BYTE length of s lies in [1, 255] inclusive -- i.e. exactly `!s.empty() && s.length() <= 255` -- applying no character-class, dot/label-structure, per-label-63, ACE-prefix ("xn--"), UTF-8-validity, or case rules at all, and reading no library global state (set_strict_mode / set_verify_dns_length do not affect it). Because the bound counts bytes rather than code points, 85 three-byte CJK characters (255 bytes) is accepted while 86 (258 bytes) is rejected; the boundary was binary-searched to largest-valid=255 / smallest-invalid=256 and confirmed in the disassembly at 0x403103 as a std::string::empty() test followed by `cmp $0xff,%rax; ja`.

to_unicode(s) removes a single leading literal ASCII "xn--" from the raw byte string s and returns the remainder, otherwise returns s verbatim: exactly `s.find("xn--") == 0 ? s.substr(4) : s` (confirmed at 0x40300a, needle literal at .rodata 0x406069). The match is byte-exact and case-sensitive ("XN--"/"Xn--"/"xN--" are left alone), anchored at offset 0 only (a prefix elsewhere in the string is never touched), and applied at most once ("xn--xn--a" -> "xn--a"); "xn--" alone yields the empty string, there is no UTF-8 decoding, no locale dependence, and no length limit or boundary of any kind.

to_lower returns a copy of the input with std::transform(..., ::tolower) applied byte-by-byte in the process's default "C" locale (main never calls setlocale), so it is strictly ASCII case folding: bytes 0x41-0x5A are shifted to 0x61-0x7A and every other byte 0x01-0x40 / 0x5B-0xFF — including all UTF-8 lead and continuation bytes, raw Latin-1 high bytes, dots, and invalid UTF-8 — is returned unchanged, preserving length exactly; it has no UTF-8/locale awareness (Turkish dotted I, Greek, and accented Latin-1 are untouched, and LC_ALL/LANG/LC_CTYPE have no effect) and no label/length limits. idna::normalize is a pure forwarder to to_lower, so field 10 is always byte-identical to field 9.

`idna::punycode_encode(s)` performs no Punycode/Bootstring encoding at all: it unconditionally returns the byte string `"xn--" + s`, concatenating the 4-byte ACE literal onto the raw input bytes with no case folding, no length limit, and no check for an already-present `xn--` prefix (so `punycode_encode("xn--a")` is `"xn--xn--a"` and the empty input yields `"xn--"`). This differs from `to_ascii(s)`, which is `"xn--" + bytewise ::tolower(s)` — the two fields diverge on any input containing `A`-`Z` (e.g. `to_ascii("ExAmPlE.CoM")` = `xn--example.com` vs `punycode_encode("ExAmPlE.CoM")` = `xn--ExAmPlE.CoM`); confirmed in the disassembly, where `0x403071` only loads the `"xn--"` literal at `0x406069` and calls `std::operator+(char const*, std::string const&)`, while `to_ascii` at `0x402f5c` first runs `std::transform(..., tolower@plt)`.

result.strategy: ascii-exhaustive differential fuzzing via a perl fork/exec driver (no python3 on this image) at /tmp/wf-fuzz-r1-0/driver.pl and /tmp/wf-fuzz-r1-0/driver2.pl. Each case builds argv as a list of raw perl byte strings and execs both binaries directly (exec {$exe} ($exe,@args)) with no shell involved, so spaces, quotes, newlines and control bytes survive verbatim. stdout is captured over a pipe and compared byte-for-byte; wait status is compared as a raw integer (so both exit code and signal death would be caught). Any candidate mismatch is re-run a second time, persisted to /tmp/wf-fuzz-r1-0/mNNNN.{c,r}.out, and independently confirmed with `cmp -s`. Groups: (A) every single byte 0x01-0x7f; (B) all 16,129 two-byte combinations over 0x01-0x7f, not just printable; (C1) exhaustive 3-byte combos over a 21-char targeted alphabet ".aAzZxXnN-0 ~!_/%+" plus TAB and LF = 9,261; (C2) 4,000 pseudo-random printable 3-byte strings; (D) every byte 0x01-0x7f inserted at start, middle and end of 5 base strings ("abcdefgh.ijklmnop", "xn--exampl.com", "WWW.Example.COM.", "....", "xn--xn--Ab"); (E) ASCII length boundaries 0..4096; (F) multi-argv and empty-argument cases; (G1) exhaustive 4-byte over the ACE alphabet "xXnN-.aA" = 4,096; (G2) 12 xn-- prefixes and near-misses ("xn--","XN--","Xn--","xN--","xn-","xn---","xn--.","-xn--",...) crossed with every ASCII byte as prefix, suffix and both; (G3) exhaustive 5-byte over "xn-.A" = 3,125; (H) 4,800 random printable strings of length 1..24; (I) 2,400 random control-char-inclusive strings over 0x01-0x7f, length 1..16; (J) length boundaries 60-68 and 250-260 in five shapes; plus the no-argument fallback path and a 7-locale LC_ALL sweep. Harness soundness was proven with two negative controls (a wrapper that tr-mutates stdout, and one that returns exit 3): both fired MISMATCH on the very first case, confirming the driver detects stdout-byte and exit-code divergence rather than silently passing.
result.notes:
CLEAN RESULT — no divergence found in 49,384 cases. Round 1 (30,271 cases) was executed twice and the two logs are byte-identical (`cmp -s run1.log run1b.log` passes), so the clean outcome is deterministic, not a flake. Runtime ~1m53s per 30k-case pass.

Confidence checks I ran so the zero is trustworthy: (1) both negative controls fired immediately, so the comparator is not vacuously passing; (2) a sanity pass over 135 inputs confirmed the C++ binary produced non-empty stdout and exit 0 for every one, i.e. no case was "matching" because both binaries silently failed to exec; (3) the 4096-byte case produces 24,600 bytes of output on both sides and compares equal, so nothing is being truncated at a pipe boundary.

Surprising/notable, all matching: input "xn--" yields empty to_unicode and punycode_decode fields, so the line contains two runs of double spaces ("xn--xn--  xn--xn--  1 1 1 0 xn-- xn-- 1") — the port reproduces the collapsed-field formatting exactly. Case-sensitivity of the prefix strip is faithful: "XN--abc" is left intact by to_unicode while to_ascii lowercases it to "xn--xn--abc". The C++ program never calls setlocale, so ::tolower stays in the "C" locale; a sweep of LC_ALL=C/POSIX/C.UTF-8/en_US.UTF-8/tr_TR.UTF-8/de_DE.UTF-8/invalid matched on all seven, including the Turkish dotless-i locale that would be the classic place for a case-folding split.

DELIBERATELY NOT COVERED — for a later reviewer:
1. High bytes 0x80-0xff, multi-byte UTF-8, and invalid/truncated UTF-8. This is the big one and it is my angle's boundary, not an oversight. Because my whole corpus is <0x80, the is_ascii_domain and is_idn_domain fields were pinned at 1 and 0 for every single case — the IDN branch was never exercised. It is also where C++ is most likely to diverge: ::tolower(char) with a negative char argument is undefined behaviour in the C++ original, and the Rust port implements it as an unconditional byte-wise to_ascii_lowercase. Someone must fuzz 0x80-0xff, especially bytes 0xC0-0xDF followed by a byte in 0x41-0x5A (an 'A'-'Z'-valued UTF-8 continuation byte), to see whether the reference glibc ::tolower leaves it alone as the port assumes.
2. NUL (0x00) is untestable through this interface at all — execve terminates argv strings at NUL, so a 0x00 byte cannot reach either main(). Group A therefore starts at 0x01 by necessity, not by choice.
3. The >255-byte-but-<255-codepoint domain case called out in the Rust doc comment for is_valid_domain (e.g. 86 CJK characters = 258 bytes) needs non-ASCII input and is unverified.
4. stderr bytes were discarded to /dev/null; only stdout and wait status were compared. If either binary writes diagnostics to stderr, that difference is invisible to me.
5. Not stressed: ARG_MAX-scale single arguments (I stopped at 4096 bytes), large argv counts (max tested was 127 elements), and 4-byte-and-longer exhaustion over the full printable set (95^4+ was out of budget — I substituted targeted ACE-alphabet exhaustion plus random sampling, so an ASCII bug needing a specific 4+ byte combination outside the "xXnN-.aA0 ~!_/%+" alphabet could still be hiding).
Artifacts: /tmp/wf-fuzz-r1-0/driver.pl, /tmp/wf-fuzz-r1-0/driver2.pl, /tmp/wf-fuzz-r1-0/sanity.pl, /tmp/wf-fuzz-r1-0/control_bytes.pl, /tmp/wf-fuzz-r1-0/control_exit.pl, logs /tmp/wf-fuzz-r1-0/run1.log, /tmp/wf-fuzz-r1-0/run1b.log, /tmp/wf-fuzz-r1-0/run2.log.

result.strategy:
Perl driver (no python3 on this image; /usr/bin/perl only) that fork/execs both binaries with list-form `exec { $bin } ($bin, @argv)` so arbitrary raw bytes reach argv without any shell re-splitting. Each run's stdout goes to its own file; comparison is `cmp -s` on those files plus a wait-status comparison that separates exit code from termination signal. Every candidate mismatch is re-run a second time and only reported if it reproduces identically.

Six rounds under /tmp/wf-fuzz-r1-5:
- fuzz.pl (6,712 cases): each of 0x01-0x1f, 0x7f, the six whitespace bytes (SP TAB LF CR VT FF) and the C1 range 0x80-0x9f — bare, doubled, x3, x7, x63, x64; each control byte leading/trailing/wrapping 13 printable hosts; interior placement; adjacency to '.'; interactions with the "xn--" ACE prefix (`\x01xn--abc` pushes the prefix off offset 0, `xn--\x01`, `X\x01N--a`, `xn-\x01-a`); 2- and 3-fold whitespace run products; dot+whitespace label-count mixes; length boundaries 0/1/2/62/63/64/65/253/254/255/256/257/300 built from whitespace and control padding; uppercase+control to_lower paths; every control x every whitespace adjacency; 600 deterministic-LCG control/whitespace soup strings; multi-arg invocations.
- fuzz2.pl (6,719) and fuzz4.pl (11,019, reseeded, 5,200 random strings up to 300 bytes): all ordered control/whitespace pairs bare and wrapped; a control byte inserted at every byte offset of "xn--host" and of "XN--HOST.Example.COM"; alternating control/'a' padding at 62/63/64/254/255/256; 1000-byte runs; `(c . ".") x 200`; CR/LF sequence families; tab/VT/FF-heavy strings; a full 0xa0-0xff sweep to exercise C++ `::tolower` on a negative `char`; every control byte x every A-Z; up to ~76-arg invocations.
- fuzz3.pl (309): extreme sizes — 4 KiB / 10 KB / 64 KiB / 100 KB / 131,000-byte single args of each whitespace and control byte (131,000 is just under Linux MAX_ARG_STRLEN), `("\n.") x 20000`, 130,000 dots to stress count_labels, a control byte at every 7th offset of a 255-byte domain, 1000-arg and 500-empty-arg invocations.
- fuzz5.pl (145,552 inputs) and fuzz6.pl (146,174 inputs): EXHAUSTIVE sweeps using batched argv (100-128 inputs per invocation, semantically safe because both drivers emit one independent line per argument) with recursive bisect-on-mismatch down to the single offending input. Covered: all 255 non-NUL single bytes bare and in four "xn--" positions; ALL 255x255 = 65,025 two-byte strings; all 44^3 three-byte strings over a control/whitespace/ACE alphabet; ALL whitespace runs of length 1-4 (1,554) in seven placements (bare, leading, trailing, both, interior, right after "xn--", prefix-displaced); ALL control-byte runs of length 1-3 over the 32 control bytes (33,824) bare, wrapped in "a...b", ACE-prefixed, and dot-joined.

Harness validated three ways before trusting any clean result: (a) substituting /bin/cat for the Rust binary made all 6,712 round-1 cases report DIFF with correct exit-code and stdout capture; (b) a wrapper that corrupts exactly one input ("\x0b\x0c") was found by the exhaustive batched sweep and bisected to precisely that one argument out of 145,552; (c) explicit verify.pl confirmed the huge-argument cases really execute (131,000 LF -> 786,024 identical stdout bytes, exit 0 both sides) rather than both silently failing exec with 127, which would have produced a false clean.

result.notes:
Clean on the assigned angle: across 316,499 inputs of control bytes, whitespace, and their mixtures with printable text, stdout was byte-identical and exit codes matched in every single case when stdout was a regular file (the harness mode the task specifies). The port is faithful here, and reading /output/src/idna/*.rs explains why — every operation is byte-level (`to_ascii_lowercase` only shifts A-Z, prefix stripping is a byte compare, lengths and dot counts are byte counts), so control bytes and whitespace are pure pass-through data with no decoding step to disagree about. Notably, the 0x80-0xff sweep also matched, which empirically confirms glibc `::tolower` on a negative `char` is identity in the C locale and that Rust's `to_ascii_lowercase` is a faithful stand-in.

About the one divergence: it is real and reproduced 6/6 across two independent repro implementations, but it is NOT input-driven — it needs stdout to be a pipe whose reader closes early, and ANY argv that produces more than one pipe buffer (~64 KiB) of output triggers it, including all-ASCII input (I first hit it with 3000 copies of "aaaa...aaaa.bbbb", also 3/3). I chose a whitespace-only argv for the reported repro to stay on my assigned angle. A reviewer should decide whether this counts in scope; the underlying port gap is that Rust std ignores SIGPIPE while the C++ binary takes the default disposition, and test11.rs additionally swallows the write error and returns success rather than dying or reporting failure.

What I deliberately did NOT cover, for later rounds to pick up:
- 0x00: cannot be passed through argv (execve NUL-terminates each element), as the task notes. I did not attempt it. Anyone wanting NUL coverage must call the library directly rather than through these drivers.
- Real UTF-8 and Unicode semantics: multi-byte CJK/emoji sequences, truncated/overlong/surrogate UTF-8, combining marks, NFC/NFD pairs, bidi controls, and Unicode whitespace (U+00A0, U+2000-200A, U+3000, U+FEFF, U+2028/2029). I only touched raw high bytes 0x80-0xff individually and a couple of continuation bytes in the soup alphabet; I never built valid multi-byte code points, so the 255-byte-vs-255-codepoint domain-length interaction and any locale-sensitive tolower on real code points are untested by me.
- Turkish/other locale effects on tolower (I never set LC_ALL / LANG; both binaries ran with the inherited environment, which was identical for both sides).
- Punycode correctness in any real sense: this library's punycode_encode/decode are just "xn--" concat and strip, so there is no Bootstring algorithm to differentially test.
- argc == 0 invocation (execve with an empty argv vector). Perl cannot construct it without raw syscalls; I only tested argc == 1, where both sides correctly fall back to the fixed trio and produce identical 222-byte output.
- Environment-level edge conditions other than the pipe case: stdout to a closed fd, to a full filesystem, to a terminal, or an fd opened O_APPEND; stdin/stderr states; resource limits (RLIMIT_FSIZE, RLIMIT_AS); and behaviour above 131,000 bytes per argument or beyond total ARG_MAX (I stayed under both limits so exec always succeeded on both sides).
- Concurrency/interleaving of the eleven API calls: single-threaded only.
Driver files, all under /tmp/wf-fuzz-r1-5: fuzz.pl, fuzz2.pl, fuzz3.pl, fuzz4.pl, fuzz5.pl, fuzz6.pl, verify.pl, repro_sigpipe.pl, plus the harness self-tests sanity.pl, fuzz5_sanity.pl and fake_rust.pl. (fuzz.py is the python3 version I wrote before discovering there is no python3 interpreter on this image; it was never executed.) Nothing under /output was modified.

result.strategy: argv-shape: exercise the CLI contract rather than the string algorithms. A Perl driver (no python3 in this image) builds each case as a full argv LIST of raw byte strings and runs both binaries via fork + block-form `exec { $bin } @list`, so arguments reach execvp verbatim with no shell splitting. stdout of each binary goes to its own file, compared with `cmp -s`; exit status is captured separately as exit<N>/sig<N> so signal deaths are distinguishable from exit codes. Every candidate mismatch is re-run and must reproduce twice before being reported (0 FLAKY lines occurred). Coverage: (1) zero arguments -> built-in default trio, repeated, plus a true argc==0 exec where argv[0] itself is absent, plus 7 odd argv[0] replacements ('', '-h', invalid UTF-8, 4KB, newline); (2) argc=1 over ~95 base tokens; (3) argc=2 as a full 30x30 pairwise sweep plus a stride sweep over all tokens; (4) argc=3 rotational sweep plus all 6 permutations of the default trio passed explicitly; (5) empty-string args alone (argc=1..14 and 50 all-empty) and mixed with non-empty via exhaustive 4-, 5-, and 6-bit empty/non-empty masks; (6) 30 flag-shaped tokens (-h, --help, -, --, -?, --HELP, -h=1, -abc, ...) each alone, before data, after data, doubled, sandwiched, and paired with an empty arg, plus all-flags-at-once and flags-interleaved-with-empties; (7) argc=10 and argc=50 mixes; (8) an arity sweep at 1,2,3,4,5,8..11,15..17,31..33,49..51,63..65,100,127..129,255..257,511,512,1000,2000,3000,5000,8000,10000,20000 in four shapes each (ascending labels / all dots / alternating empty / all 0xff); (9) a single 60KB argument at 60KB-1, 60KB, 60KB+1 and at 1K..100K, in 11 byte patterns (a, dot, 0xff, upper, 2-byte UTF-8, xn--, a-dot, newline, tab, space, dash), alone and mixed with 'one' and with empty args, plus four 60KB args, ten 16KB args, fifty 4KB args; (10) per-argument size walked right up to the kernel MAX_ARG_STRLEN boundary (131060..131073); (11) every byte value 0x01..0xff as a lone one-byte argument and all 18x18 two-byte combinations of interesting bytes; (12) 1200 randomized cases at random arity 0..60 plus 540 at the arities named in the brief. Finally, stdout disposition was varied while holding argv fixed: file, /dev/full, closed fd, and pipe with an early-exiting reader.

result.notes:
HARNESS WAS VALIDATED BEFORE TRUSTING THE CLEAN RESULT. selftest.pl (/tmp/wf-fuzz-r1-7/selftest.pl) confirms the comparison logic reports DIFF when one binary is swapped for /usr/bin/printf, and that run_bin correctly distinguishes exit42, sig11, and exit127. verify.pl and verify2.pl confirm the big/high-arity cases were non-vacuous rather than silently failing to exec: the 60KB single-arg case yields 368664 identical bytes from both binaries, argc=2000 yields 2000 matching lines, argc=20000 yields 1133364 matching bytes, four 60KB args yield 1474656 matching bytes, and the true argc==0 exec yields the 222-byte default trio from both.

ONLY DIVERGENCE IS SIGPIPE DISPOSITION, NOT ARGV HANDLING. Across all 4400+ file-redirected cases, stdout was byte-identical and exit codes matched everywhere: zero stdout divergences, zero FLAKY cases, zero saved mismatch artifacts. The single finding is a process-level signal-disposition difference (C++ leaves SIGPIPE at SIG_DFL; the Rust runtime sets SIG_IGN) that only manifests when stdout is a pipe whose reader exits early AND the output exceeds the 64KB pipe buffer. It is arguably a runtime artifact rather than a port bug in the idna logic, but it is a real, deterministically reproduced exit-code divergence under identical argv, so I am reporting it. Fixing it would require restoring SIG_DFL for SIGPIPE at the top of main. Note it is timing-dependent for small outputs: at argc=100 (~2.5KB, fits the pipe buffer) it fired in only 1 of 3 reps, so a reviewer should use argc>=1000 or the 60KB argument for a deterministic repro.

INCIDENTAL ENVIRONMENT FACTS. The kernel refuses any single argument of 131072 bytes or more (MAX_ARG_STRLEN), and refuses total argv above roughly 2MB; those cases were flagged VACUOUS by driver3.pl because exec failed identically (exit127) for both binaries, so they prove nothing. Real coverage therefore stops at 131071 bytes per argument, comfortably above the 60KB the brief asked for. A NUL byte cannot appear inside an argv element at all, so 0x00 is untestable through argv; byte coverage is 0x01..0xff.

DELIBERATELY NOT COVERED, for a later reviewer to pick up. (a) The string algorithms themselves -- punycode/ACE semantics, the 63/255 length thresholds, tolower edge cases, UTF-8 boundary behaviour. I used many such strings as argv payloads, but I did not systematically target the algorithm boundaries; that belongs to a content-oriented strategy. (b) stderr content was captured and observed empty for every non-vacuous case, but I did not diff stderr byte-for-byte as a pass/fail criterion, per the brief's stdout+exit-code contract. (c) Environment variables, locale (LC_ALL / LANG affecting the C++ tolower path), working directory, umask, and stdin content -- all left at the inherited defaults; a locale-sensitivity sweep is a plausible next angle since the Rust port hardcodes C-locale ASCII-only case folding. (d) Resource-limit interactions: ulimit -v / -s / RLIMIT_FSIZE / RLIMIT_STACK were untouched, so allocation-failure paths on multi-megabyte arguments are unexplored, as is the i32 return type of count_labels (reaching INT_MAX dots would need a 2GB argument, unreachable through argv). (e) Concurrency, non-Linux platforms, and the /output/target/release/test11 copy (I tested /output/test11 only; they appear to be the same 13249528-byte build).

result.strategy:
Strategy "ace-prefix": programmatic differential fuzzing of /workspace/dataset/test11_executable (C++ ground truth) vs /output/test11 (Rust port), with every mutation built around the "xn--" ACE prefix. Driver written in perl (no python3 on this box) at /tmp/wf-fuzz-r1-3/fuzz.pl, /tmp/wf-fuzz-r1-3/round2.pl, /tmp/wf-fuzz-r1-3/round3.pl, /tmp/wf-fuzz-r1-3/round4.pl. Each case is passed as raw bytes in a SINGLE argv element via fork + `exec { $bin } ($bin, @args)` (list form, never a shell, never re-split); stdout and stderr are redirected to separate files in the child and compared with `cmp -s`; wait status is compared for both exit code and killing signal.

Harness was validated with controls first (/tmp/wf-fuzz-r1-3/sanity.pl): cpp-vs-cpp reports SAME, cpp-vs-/bin/echo reports DIFF (so the comparator can actually fail), /bin/false exit code is captured, and a raw 0xff byte survives the argv round-trip into the output.

Four rounds:
1. Round 1 (7032 cases): ~58 prefix variants (all case permutations of x/n crossed with 0-5 dashes; truncations "", x, X, n, N, -, --, ---; dash-displaced forms x-n--, xn.-, xn_-, xn -, xnn--, xn---x, nx--; near-miss bytes \xf8n--, x\xee--, xn\x2d\xad, en-dash and fullwidth "xn") crossed with 48 bodies, plus prefix-only, prefix+1char over 23 chars, repetition 1-8x for 7 flavours, embedding at every offset of 5 carriers, per-label templates (a.xn--b, xn--a.xn--b, xn--.a.xn--.b.xn--), trailing/leading dot runs 0-8, 63/255 length boundaries, exotic sequences (ZWSP, BOM, soft hyphen, overlong NUL, ideographic/fullwidth full stop, emoji, lone surrogate), and a full 1-255 single-byte sweep in 5 positions around the prefix.
2. Round 2 (4709 cases): huge inputs, exhaustive byte 1-255 as whole body after 13 prefix flavours, one argv holding all 255 non-NUL bytes, prefix repetition up to 4096 copies, upper-case prefix glued to high bytes (to exercise ::tolower on a negative char), exact thresholds 58-68 and 250-260, and 1-1024 argv elements.
3. Round 3 (190 cases): the exact MAX_ARG_STRLEN ceiling (131071-byte args, the largest that actually exec) plus total-ARG_MAX pressure spread over 2-32 args.
4. Round 4 (14792 cases): exhaustive enumeration of EVERY string over the ACE-relevant alphabets - {x,X,n,N,-,.} for all lengths 0-5, and {x,n,-,\xff} for all lengths 0-6. This proves the prefix detect/strip logic by exhaustion rather than sampling.

Plus 45 targeted exit-code probes with stdout as a pipe closed early by the reader.

divergences.reproCommand: A="xn--$(perl -e 'print "a" x 20000')"; /workspace/dataset/test11_executable "$A" 2>/dev/null | head -c 5 >/dev/null; echo "cpp_exit=${PIPESTATUS[0]}"; /output/test11 "$A" 2>/dev/null | head -c 5 >/dev/null; echo "rust_exit=${PIPESTATUS[0]}"   # bash, needs PIPESTATUS
divergences.cppOutput: cpp_exit=141 (killed by signal 13, SIGPIPE). The 5 bytes actually delivered to the consumer are identical to Rust's.
divergences.rustOutput: rust_exit=0 (exits cleanly). Deterministic 5/5 runs at every arg length >= ~2000, and re-verified twice more; C++ is always 141, Rust always 0.

result.notes:
MAIN RESULT: zero divergences on the ace-prefix angle. Under the comparison protocol specified for this task (input as a single argv element, stdout captured to files, compared with `cmp -s`, exit codes compared), all 26,723 systematic cases matched byte-exactly, including the round-4 exhaustive enumeration of every string over {x,X,n,N,-,.} up to length 5 and {x,n,-,\xff} up to length 6. The Rust port's prefix handling is byte-faithful: `strip_prefix(b"xn--")` in /output/src/idna/convert.rs matches the C++ `s.find("xn--") == 0 ? s.substr(4) : s` on every input I could construct, including the case-sensitivity (XN-- is NOT stripped), all truncations, and the empty string.

ABOUT THE ONE REPORTED DIVERGENCE - read this before treating it as an ace-prefix bug. It is real and fully deterministic, but it is NOT prefix-specific and does NOT appear under the file-redirect protocol:
  - It reproduces identically with a plain non-prefixed argument (20000 'a's, no "xn--"), so it is an I/O/runtime difference, not ACE-prefix logic. I used an xn-- argument only because that is the angle I was fuzzing.
  - With stdout redirected to a file (the protocol above), the same argv gives cpp=0, rust=0 and byte-identical 120040-byte stdout. The divergence needs stdout to be a pipe whose reader closes early AND output large enough that a second write() syscall happens after the close.
  - Mechanism: Rust's std runtime sets SIGPIPE to SIG_IGN before main, so the write returns EPIPE; /output/test11.rs lines 49-51 then swallow it (`if out.write_all(&line).is_err() { return; }`) and main falls off the end with status 0. The C++ binary keeps the default SIGPIPE disposition and is killed by signal 13. Whether this counts as a port defect is a judgement call for the reviewer; I am reporting it because exit-code comparison was explicitly in scope and it reproduced every single time.

HARNESS ARTIFACT, NOT A FINDING: round 2 logged 20 "stderr diffs", all in the `huge` tag. Cause is that arguments of >=131072 bytes exceed MAX_ARG_STRLEN, so `exec` fails with E2BIG before either binary runs, and perl's error text embeds the binary path, whose length differs ("/workspace/dataset/test11_executable" vs "/output/test11"). Neither program executed; stdout and wait status matched. Round 3 then confirmed the largest args that DO exec (131071 bytes) match cleanly. Outside those E2BIG cases, stderr was byte-identical (both empty) in every case; neither binary ever wrote to stderr, and neither ever crashed, hung, or produced a nonzero exit under file-redirected stdout.

DELIBERATELY NOT COVERED (for a later reviewer / other rounds):
  - Non-ACE angles: I did not systematically fuzz the length predicates (is_valid_domain 255 / is_valid_label 63) away from the prefix, the count_labels dot counter on dot-dense inputs unrelated to "xn--", or to_lower/normalize over non-prefixed text. I hit these incidentally as output fields on every one of the 26k cases, but they were not the mutation target.
  - NUL bytes inside an argument: impossible to pass through execve, so untestable via argv. 0 cases were actually skipped for this reason since my generators never emitted a NUL.
  - Locale effects on ::tolower: I only ran under the inherited default locale. Running with LC_ALL/LANG set to a non-C locale (e.g. tr_TR.UTF-8 or a single-byte 8-bit locale) could make the C++ `::tolower` fold bytes >=0x80 that the Rust `to_ascii_lowercase` leaves alone. This is the most promising untested lead I am aware of and I recommend it as a follow-up angle.
  - Multi-byte/UTF-8 semantic correctness of real punycode: irrelevant here, since both implementations are stub string concatenations rather than actual punycode codecs.
  - Environment-dependent behaviour other than the pipe case: no tests with stdout on a full filesystem, a non-blocking fd, or a tty.
  - I did not diff argv handling above 1024 arguments, nor total ARG_MAX exhaustion beyond ~100 KB spread across 32 args.

Scratch dir with all drivers and logs: /tmp/wf-fuzz-r1-3 (fuzz.pl, round2.pl, round3.pl, round4.pl, sanity.pl, probe.pl, full.log, full2.log, full4.log). Nothing under /output was modified.

result.strategy:
Six perl-based differential rounds (no python3 on the box), each forking and exec'ing both binaries with list-form argv so raw bytes pass through untouched by any shell. Every case captured stdout to separate files and compared with byte equality plus full wait status; any mismatch was re-run twice more and discarded as FLAKY unless it reproduced identically both times.

R1 (2971 cases, structured): only-dots strings length 0..40 plus probes at 60/62/63/64/65/100/127/128/200/254/255/256/257/300/512/1000; leading dots 0..24 prefixed to a, a.b, xn--a, XN--A; trailing dots 0..24 on a, a.b, xn--a, xn--, XN--; doubled/tripled interior dots 0..15 between a|b, AB|CD, xn--|xn--; cartesian 2-way (21x21) and 3-way (9x9x9) dot-joins over empty/ASCII/uppercase/UTF-8/invalid-byte/whitespace/quote labels; a., .a, ab., ..a repeated 1..140 to cross the 63 and 255 byte bounds; exact-length strings at 1,2,3,61-66,126-128,253-258,300 built from 8 dot patterns; 17 xn-- prefix variants each with lead/trail/mid dot runs 0..5; 22 raw/invalid byte sequences in 9 dot templates; label counts 1..2000; case-folding boundary chars @[`{ around dots; 10 multi-argv batches.

R2 (4604 cases, exhaustive byte coverage): every byte 0x01..0xFF placed in 13 dot templates, plus every byte doubled around a dot and wrapped in A..Z; extreme-length dot strings at 1000..131071 (Linux MAX_ARG_STRLEN); label counts to 65535; 2..1000 argv elements of dot arrangements; dots straddling every cut point of 4 multi-byte UTF-8 sequences; dot swept through every position of 63/64/255/256-byte strings.

R3 (4900 cases x 2 stdout modes = 9800 comparisons): seeded-random dot-heavy strings over a 28-symbol alphabet weighted 4:1 toward '.', random empty/non-empty label joins, random multi-argv batches — each run with stdout to a regular file AND with stdout to a fully drained pipe.

R4 (190 comparisons): early-closed-pipe matrix — reader consumes N of {1,5,100,4096,65536} bytes then closes, over dots lengths 0..131071 and 1..6000 argv elements.

R5 (16930 cases, EXHAUSTIVE): enumerated every string over {'.','a'} len 1..12, {'.','a','A'} len 1..7, {'.','x','n','-'} len 1..6, plus the empty string. This is total coverage of all possible dot arrangements at short lengths.

R6 (1386 cases): LC_ALL/LC_CTYPE/LANG sweep over 14 locales (C, POSIX, C.utf8, en_US.utf8/iso88591, de_DE.iso88591, tr_TR.utf8/iso88599, ru_RU.koi8r, ja_JP.eucjp, zh_CN.gb18030, lt_LT.utf8, az_AZ.utf8, el_GR.iso88597) crossed with dot-separated high bytes and dotted/dotless-I cases, probing whether C++ ::tolower diverges from the Rust port's hardcoded ASCII fold.

Also spot-checked the zero-argument default-trio path and the documented example inputs.

divergences.cppOutput: cpp_exit=141  (process killed by SIGPIPE, i.e. wait status signal 13). Bytes the reader received: "xn--." (5 bytes, identical to Rust).
divergences.rustOutput: rust_exit=0  (process exits normally). Bytes the reader received: "xn--." (5 bytes, identical to C++).

result.notes:
THE DOTS-AND-LABELS ANGLE IS CLEAN. Across 35,916 comparisons — including a genuinely exhaustive enumeration of every dot arrangement over {'.','a'} up to length 12 (8190 strings), {'.','a','A'} up to length 7 (3279), and {'.','x','n','-'} up to length 6 (5460) — all eleven API columns (to_ascii, to_unicode, punycode_encode, punycode_decode, is_valid_domain, is_valid_label, is_ascii_domain, is_idn_domain, to_lower, normalize, count_labels) matched byte-for-byte with identical exit codes whenever stdout was a file or a fully drained pipe. Zero FLAKY results outside the pipe-race cases in R4. The 63-byte and 255-byte validator boundaries, the xn-- prefix strip (including case-sensitivity: XN-- is correctly left alone by both), byte-wise tolower over all 255 non-NUL byte values, and count_labels over 1..131072 dots all agree exactly.

THE ONE DIVERGENCE IS NOT DOTS-SPECIFIC — it is a SIGPIPE disposition difference, and it also reproduces with a non-dot control (an argv element of 8000 'a' bytes gives cpp_exit=141 / rust_exit=0 too). The C++ binary keeps the default SIGPIPE handler and dies with signal 13 the moment a stdout write fails; the Rust runtime installs SIG_IGN for SIGPIPE at startup, so write_all returns EPIPE and /output/test11.rs's `if out.write_all(&line).is_err() { return; }` swallows it and falls through to exit 0. Root-cause note for the fixer: the C++ driver also *continues its loop* after a failed write (std::cout just sets badbit) whereas the Rust driver returns immediately, so behaviour would still differ on a non-fatal stdout error even if SIGPIPE were restored. Triggering needs >64 KiB of output so the pipe buffer fills after the reader closes; the threshold sits between 1000 and 8000 dots in a single argv element (measured: 1000 dots -> both 0; 8000 dots -> 141 vs 0). R4 observed 118 instances of this single root cause across the length x reader-size matrix, and in ALL 118 the stdout bytes were identical — the divergence is purely in the wait status. I am reporting it as one divergence, not 118. Note that with output under ~64 KiB the outcome is timing-dependent (3 FLAKY entries in R4 at small sizes), which is why the repro deliberately uses 8000 dots, where it is deterministic — verified 3/3 on the exact repro command and 3/3 on a 5000-argv variant.

Locale is a dead end and can be crossed off: the C++ binary never calls setlocale, so it stays in the "C" locale no matter what LC_ALL/LC_CTYPE/LANG say. All 1386 locale x high-byte cases matched, including Turkish dotted/dotless I (tr_TR) and Greek/Cyrillic 8-bit charsets, which are where a locale-sensitive ::tolower would have broken the Rust port's hardcoded ASCII fold.

DELIBERATELY NOT COVERED, for a later reviewer to pick up:
- NUL bytes inside an argv element. Impossible via execve; unreachable through this interface by construction, so the C++ std::string vs Rust Vec<u8> length semantics can never be distinguished here.
- argv elements longer than 131071 bytes (Linux MAX_ARG_STRLEN) and total argv beyond ~6000 elements — the kernel rejects these before either binary runs.
- Non-dot semantic angles that belong to other fuzz shards: real IDN/punycode round-trip corpora, Unicode normalization and non-ASCII case folding as *semantics* (I only covered them at the byte level incidentally via the all-255-bytes matrix), and the 4-byte/astral-plane code point space beyond the 4 sequences used in the split tests.
- stderr contents. I redirected stderr to /dev/null throughout and never compared it; neither binary appeared to write there, but that is unverified.
- Other write-error stdout dispositions: I tested regular files, fully drained pipes, and early-closed pipes, but NOT /dev/full (ENOSPC), a closed fd 1, a full tty, or a non-blocking stdout. /dev/full in particular is worth a look — it should expose the "C++ continues the loop, Rust returns early" asymmetry described above on a multi-argv input, and I did not execute it.
- stdin and environment variables other than the locale trio.
- Repeated/concurrent invocation or any cross-run state.

result.strategy:
Strategy "length-boundaries", implemented as three Perl drivers in /tmp/wf-fuzz-r1-1 (no python3 on this box; Perl's list-form `open(FH,'-|',$prog,@args)` gives exact byte-level argv control with no shell re-splitting). Each case spawns /workspace/dataset/test11_executable and /output/test11 with byte-identical argv, slurps stdout in binmode, and compares raw bytes plus decoded exit status.

Round 1 (driver.pl, 1026 cases): lengths 0..300 of plain "a"; 2-byte (U+00E9), 3-byte (U+65E5), 4-byte (U+1F600) UTF-8 repeated at char counts chosen so BYTE length lands on 61..66 and 253..258 while char count does not (e.g. 85 CJK chars = 255 bytes vs 86 = 258 bytes); mixed MB+ASCII padding hitting every exact byte length 58..69 and 248..261; deliberately TRUNCATED multi-byte sequences so the string is invalid UTF-8 with its split point exactly at 62/63/64/65/254/255/256/257 bytes; dots straddling boundaries (leading, trailing, both, all-dots, alternating, and a single dot walked to 11 offsets); dot+multibyte so byte length crosses 63/255 while char count stays under; "xn--"/"XN--"/"xn--xn--" prefixes truncated to 0..7, 62..68, 253..260 bytes (exercises the 4-byte strip in to_unicode/punycode_decode against the boundary); uppercase, 0xFF, 0x80, 0x7F, newline, tab, space, quote, backslash fills at each boundary; single high byte at head/tail of a 62..257-byte ASCII run (flips is_ascii_domain exactly at the boundary).

Round 1b (driver2.pl, 5699 cases): dense sweep — EVERY byte length 0..320 for each of the three MB units truncated to that length, and for six mixed patterns ("a.", CJK+".", "a\xc3\xa9.\xe6\x97\xa5", "A"+emoji+".", "xn--", "\xff\x80"); a dot at EVERY position 0..b-1 for total lengths exactly 63/64/255/256; every single byte value 0x01..0xFF placed at head and tail of 63/64/255/256-byte strings; power-of-two and large lengths (500..131072) for a/dot/CJK/0xFF/uppercase/xn-- fills; count_labels stress with 255..200000 dots.

Round 1c (driver3.pl, 2887 cases): label-structure lengths — labels of every length L in 1..70 joined by dots and truncated to exact totals 60..68 and 250..260, each also with trailing dot stripped and doubled; CJK labels of 18..24 chars (21 chars = exactly 63 bytes) alone, dotted, and repeated x2/x4/x5 to straddle 255; "xn--" + body of 55..72 and 246..264 bytes in ASCII/uppercase/CJK/dotted forms; multi-arg invocations of 2/3/4/8/16 args each at a boundary length plus mixed/empty/high-byte sets; ascending arg-length ladders 0..80 and 240..280 in a single invocation; 200/500/1000-arg invocations.

Negative control: re-ran round 1 with /output/test11 replaced by a wrapper piping its stdout through `tr a b`. The harness reported 821 of 1026 as MISMATCH, confirming the byte comparison and reporting path actually fire.

Determinism: all three rounds were executed twice end to end. Both passes returned 0 mismatches.
result.notes:
CLEAN RESULT — no divergence found. 9612 unique argv sets, each executed twice (19224 total both-binary comparisons); 0 stdout-byte or exit-code mismatches in either pass. No artifact files were written to the mismatch dirs /tmp/wf-fuzz-r1-1/out2 and /tmp/wf-fuzz-r1-1/out3 (both empty); /tmp/wf-fuzz-r1-1/out contains only the 2463 files from the deliberate negative-control run.

Drivers (re-runnable): /tmp/wf-fuzz-r1-1/driver.pl, /tmp/wf-fuzz-r1-1/driver2.pl, /tmp/wf-fuzz-r1-1/driver3.pl. Run with `perl <path>`; each prints only mismatches plus a final total. /tmp/wf-fuzz-r1-1/driver.py is the original Python version, kept for a future environment that has python3 — it was never executed here.

Confirmed the boundaries were genuinely crossed rather than merely generated: at 85 CJK chars (255 bytes) the 5th field is_valid_domain prints 1, at 86 chars (258 bytes) it prints 0, and both binaries agree. Likewise is_valid_label's 6th field flips between 63 and 64 bytes. So the sweep is exercising the real 63/255 byte-length predicates and confirming the Rust port measures bytes (not chars), matching C++ std::string::length().

Environment limit worth recording: execve enforces MAX_ARG_STRLEN = 131072, so a single argv element of 131072+ bytes fails to spawn. Verified 131071 bytes works for both (786450 bytes of identical stdout, exit 0) and 131072 fails for both (exit 126, empty stdout) — identical behaviour, so not a divergence, but it means single-argument lengths at or above 131072 bytes are UNTESTABLE through this driver on this platform. Roughly 8 round-1b cases (the >=131072 and 200000-byte ones) hit this and were effectively skipped, both sides returning the same spawn-fail sentinel.

DELIBERATELY NOT COVERED, for a later reviewer to pick up:
1. NUL bytes inside an argument. Impossible via argv (execve terminates at NUL), so any NUL-truncation difference between std::string and Vec<u8> cannot be reached from this driver — it would need a different entry point.
2. The zero-argument default path (argc == 1 -> the fixed {"one","two.three","four.five.six"} trio). Every case here passed at least one argument. Trivially checkable but outside a length sweep.
3. Semantic/content fuzzing unrelated to length: punycode-ish payloads, real IDN test vectors, Unicode normalization forms (NFC vs NFD), surrogate-range and overlong UTF-8 encodings chosen for their meaning rather than their byte count, case-folding of non-ASCII letters (Turkish dotless i, sigma). I only used such bytes as length filler.
4. Locale sensitivity of ::tolower. All runs inherited the default environment; I did not vary LC_ALL/LC_CTYPE. If the C++ side is locale-sensitive and the Rust side hard-codes ASCII-only folding, a non-C locale plus high bytes is where they would split. This is the most promising untested angle I noticed.
5. stdout-to-non-tty vs tty buffering. All stdout was captured through a pipe. Behaviour on a pty, and behaviour under a short/failing write (EPIPE, full disk) where the Rust driver silently `return`s on write_all error while C++ std::cout sets badbit, is untested.
6. Interleaving of stdout with stderr. Neither binary wrote to stderr in any case, and I compared stdout only.
7. Arg-count extremes beyond 1000 args, and total-argv-block sizes near the ~2 MB ARG_MAX aggregate ceiling.
8. Signals, resource limits, and allocation failure under the very large (65 KB..128 KB) inputs — outputs matched, but I did not constrain memory to probe OOM paths.
